arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Robbins argued for the sides that brought the case. He focused on clear state conditions. He cited the Arlington Central School District case. He emphasized the importance of clear federal instructions.
Mr. Snyder argued for the opposing sides. He emphasized the text of Section 1983. He argued the statute provides an express cause of action. He cited half a century of precedent.

Mr. Fisher argued for the sides that brought the case. He highlighted the unpredictability of current law. He argued this frustrates state assessment of programs. He noted the disruption to state resource administration.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the scope of Section 1983. It asks if this statute covers rights created by federal spending programs. The outcome affects how states manage federal funds and how individuals seek redress.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the sides that brought the case want the Court to limit Section 1983. They seek to prevent suits based on spending clause conditions. They argue this protects state administrative flexibility.
the opposing sides want the Court to expand Section 1983. They seek to allow suits for any federal statutory right. They argue this ensures accountability for federal conditions.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the sides that brought the case argue Section 1983 does not cover spending clause rights. They claim this interpretation frustrates state program administration. They cite the need for clear state conditions.
the opposing sides argue Section 1983 covers all federal statutory rights. They claim the statute text supports this broad reading. They argue precedent supports this interpretation.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Kavanaugh asked how to address prior precedent. He noted state remedies do not usually block Section 1983 suits. He asked the advocate to respond to this point.
